o: Right to Freedom of trade and profession
Protection of life and personal liberty
28.x: The Right to Freedom of trade, profession, occupation, or business under Article 19 is available only to Indian citizens

28.s: Which Article of the Constitution of India is related with Freedom of the Press.
28.x: In the Indian Constitution, freedom of the Press is not given directly, but the Supreme Court held that the right to freedom of speech and expression [Article 19 (1)(a)] includes the right to freedom of the Press.

28.s:
Which of the following rights is/are not included in the ‘Right to Freedom’ under Article 19(1) ?
1. Right of equal opportunities
2. Right to assemble peaceably
3. Right to practise any profession
4. Freedom of speech and expression
28.x: According to Article 19(1), among the given statements, the rights that fall under Article 19(1) are: (b) Right to assemble peacefully and without arms; (g) Right to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business; (a) Freedom of speech and expression; Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment (Article 16) is not included under the Right to Freedom; it is under the right to equality.

28.s: Which of the follwing freedoms is not guaranteed by the Indian Constitution under Article 19?
o: Freedom to assemble peacefully and without arms
Freedom to own, acquire and dispose of property
Freedom to move freely throughout the country
Freedom to practise any trade or profession
28.x: The Article 19 (Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.) under fundamental rights mentioned in part III of the Constitution provides guarantee of the following 6 freedoms by clause (1) as the right- (a) to freedom of Speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; and (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. It is noteworthy that, the freedom to own, acquire and dispose of a property was included in Article 19 clause (1) sub-clause (f) under the initial/original constitution, but the 44th Amendment of the Constitution, 1978 removed this sub-clause (f) from the Article 19(1).

28.s: A British citizen staying in India cannot claim right to –
o: Protection of life and Personal Liberty
28.x: A British citizen staying in India cannot claim 'Right to Freedom of Trade and Profession' because the Right which has been provided under Article 19(1)(g) is available only to the citizens of India, but the other three rights given in the options are available to every person.

28.s: As a part of the Right to Freedom, which one of the followings does not form part of “Freedom to Assemble Peaceably and Without Arms”?
o: Gherao officials not performing their duties
People who assemble should not bear arms
State can make a law imposing reasonable restrictions
28.x: Article 19(1)(b) provides the freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms, and under Article 19(3), the state can impose reasonable restrictions on it in the interest of public order.

28.s: Freedom of News Papers in India-
o: Has origin by the enforcement of Rule of law
28.x: Freedom of the Newspapers or Press is not directly provided by the Constitution but is included in Article 19(1)(a) as freedom of speech and expression. In the case of Sakal Papers Ltd. Vs. Union of India, 1961, the Supreme Court stated that the freedom of the Press is included in the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

28.s: A British Citizen staying in India can not claim right to
o: Protection of life and personal liberty
28.x: In India, certain Fundamental Rights are exclusively available to citizens, while others extend to all individuals, including foreign nationals. A British citizen residing in India cannot claim the right to "freedom of trade and profession" as enshrined in Article 19(1)(g) of the Indian Constitution, which is reserved solely for Indian citizens.

28.s:
Consider the following statements: No one can be compelled to sing the National Anthem since:
1. It will be violative of the Right to freedom of speech and expression.
2. It will be violative of the Right to freedom of conscience and practise and propagation of religion.
3. There is no legal provision obliging anyone to sing the National Anthem. Of these statements:
28.x: All three statements are correct: In Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986), the Supreme Court held that compelling students to sing the National Anthem against their sincerely held religious beliefs infringed upon their Fundamental Rights. The Court ruled that such compulsion violates the Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression under Article 19(1)(a) as well as the Freedom of Conscience and the Right to Profess and Practise Religion under Article 25(1). Further, the Court observed that there is no law or statutory provision mandating individuals to sing the National Anthem. • It also clarified that Article 51A(a), which enjoins citizens to respect the National Flag and National Anthem, constitutes a Fundamental Duty and is not enforceable through legal compulsion. Additionally, while the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act penalises the intentional disruption or obstruction of the singing of the National Anthem, it does not criminalise respectful non-participation by individuals acting in accordance with their conscientious beliefs.

28.s: Which Article of the Indian Constitution protects person’s right to travel abroad:
28.x: In the case of Maneka Gandhi Vs. UOI, 1978, the Supreme Court held that the right to travel abroad is a fundamental right and is secured by Article 21.

28.s: The Supreme Court has held that hoisting the National Flag atop the private buildings is a fundamental right of every citizen under:
28.x: According to the Supreme Court of India, hoisting the national Flag atop private buildings is a fundamental right of every citizen under Article 19 (1)(a) of the Constitution. Article 14 guarantees equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws. Article 21 deals with the right to life and personal liberty. Article 25 provides for freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion.

28.s: Which Article of the Constitution ensure the freedom of the Press?
In which Article the Fundamental Rights to Freedom of Speech and Expression is provided in the Constitution of India?

Choose the fundamental rights available to Indian Citizen but not to aliens:
I. Freedom of Speech and Expression
II. Equality Before the Law
III. Right of Minorities
IV. Protection of Life and Liberty
28.x: The Right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19, and the cultural and educational rights of minorities under Article 29, are available to Indian citizens only. They are not available to aliens/foreigners.

28.s:
Reasonable restrictions on 'Exercise of Freedom of Speech and Expression' under Article 19(2) are justified in the interest of which of the following conditions?
I. Security of State
II. Defamation
III. Sedition
IV. Public order
Select the correct answer :
28.x: Reasonable restrictions on the Exercise of Freedom of Speech and Expression under Article 19(2) are justified in the interest of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the state, friendly relations with foreign states, Public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

28.s:
The constitution of India provides for reasonable restrictions on Fundamental Rights but reasonableness must keep in mind that:
1) The interest of the general public is safeguarded
2) Prevailing social value and also social needs are not bar
3) Directive principles can be bypassed
4) Collective good is not greater Out of these:
28.x: Under Article 19, the freedoms granted (speech and expression, forming associations, free movement, etc.) may be subjected to reasonable restrictions by the State through law. Articles 19(2) to 19(6) provide that such limits may be imposed only for certain specified objectives—such as the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency or morality, protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes, and professional/technical regulations, etc. Therefore, only statements 1 and 2 align with the constitutional and judicial tests of reasonable restrictions, whereas statements 3 and 4 are both incorrect.

28.s: Which of the following is not a fundamental right granted by the Indian Constitution to the citizens?
o: Right to Settle in any part of the Country
28.x: According to the decision of the Supreme Court, the Right to information lies in the Right to freedom of speech and expression under Art. 19 (1) (a) of the Constitution of India. Although, it is not mentioned in the Constitution of India.

28.s: Which one of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution belongs to a different category:
28.x: The right to freedom is granted in the Indian Constitution from (Articles 19 -22), where Article 19 deals with the protection of certain rights including the right to freedom of speech, peaceful assembly, form association or union or co-operative society, move freely throughout the territory, settle and reside, etc. Article 20 deals with protection in respect of conviction for offences, Article 21 deals with the right to life and personal liberty, Article 21-A deals with right to education, Article 22 deals with protection against arrest and detention in certain circumstances.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about protections under Article 20:
1. The protection under Article 20(1) against a heavier penalty than that applicable when the offence was committed applies to criminal laws.
2. Article 20(2) does not bar departmental proceedings after a criminal conviction for the same act.
3. The expression 'procedure established by law' is associated with the constitution of Japan.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Article 20(1) applies to criminal laws; it bars conviction and a greater penalty, but not necessarily the trial itself.
Statement 2: Correct: Article 20(2) covers only prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal, not departmental proceedings.
Statement 3: Correct: 'procedure established by law' is associated with Japan, while 'due process' is associated with the United States.

29.s:
With reference to Article 20(3), consider the following statements:
1. It applies to criminal proceedings.
2. It covers oral and documentary testimony.
3. It generally treats fingerprints and physical specimens as testimonial self-incrimination.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Physical evidence such as fingerprints is not treated as testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3), as recognised in Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961).
29.tq: Separate testimonial evidence from physical evidence before selecting the combination.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Art. 20(3)** applies only to **criminal proceedings**.
Statement 2 correct: it covers **oral and documentary testimony**.
Statement 3 wrong: **physical evidence** like **fingerprints/specimens** is not covered (**Kathi Kalu Oghad 1961**).
xa: **Selvi v State of Karnataka (2010):** **narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping** without consent violate 20(3).
20(3) means an accused **cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself**.
Art. 20 protections are **non-suspendable** in an emergency.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about the scope of Article 21:
1. The protection under Article 21 is available to citizens only.
2. Compared with A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 also protects against arbitrary legislative action.
3. The right to a clean environment and air was read into Article 21 in Subhash Kumar.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: Article 21 protects both citizens and non-citizens.
Statement 2: Correct: A.K. Gopalan read Article 21 narrowly; Maneka Gandhi extended protection against arbitrary legislative action.
Statement 3: Correct: Subhash Kumar recognised a clean environment; Olga Tellis gave shelter and livelihood.

29.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 21 – Preventive detention and safeguards against arrest
Article 20 – Protection in respect of conviction for offences
Article 21A – Protection against ex post facto criminal laws
Article 22 – Free education for children aged six to fourteen
29.x: Article 20 protects in respect of conviction for offences; Article 21 covers life and liberty, 21A education and 22 arrest and detention.
xa: Art. 20's three protections: **no ex post facto law**, **no double jeopardy**, **no self-incrimination**.
Art. 20 is available to **citizens, foreigners and companies**; **non-suspendable** in emergency.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 20 and arrest safeguards:
1. In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that narco-analysis, polygraph tests and brain-mapping conducted without consent violate Article 20(3).
2. The protections under Article 20 are available to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies.
3. BNSS Sections 22 and 24 broadly correspond to CrPC Sections 50 and 57 on grounds of arrest and production before a magistrate.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Selvi (2010) held these tests without consent violate the protection against testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).
Statement 2: Correct: Article 20 protections extend to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies, subject to the nature of each protection.
Statement 3: Incorrect: it is BNSS Sections 47 and 58 that broadly correspond to CrPC Sections 50 and 57.

29.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 21 uses the expression 'procedure established by law'.
2. A.K. Gopalan (1950) held a law valid if enacted through correct legislative procedure.
3. After Maneka Gandhi (1978), a law must also be just, fair and reasonable.
Which of the above statements are correct?
29.x: All three are correct: Article 21 says 'procedure established by law', Gopalan required only proper enactment, and Maneka Gandhi added 'just, fair and reasonable'.
n: The phrase “Procedure Established by Law” appears in the text of Article 21. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Under procedure established by law, a law is valid if it is enacted according to the correct legislative procedure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The procedure-established-by-law approach was stated in A.K. Gopalan in 1950. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
After Maneka Gandhi in 1978, due process of law requires a law to be just, fair, and reasonable. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
After Maneka Gandhi, due process of law requires freedom from procedural arbitrariness. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xa: "Procedure established by law" came from the **Japanese** Constitution; **due process** from the **USA**.
**Gopalan** treated Arts. 19, 21, 22 as **separate**; **Maneka** linked **14, 19, 21** — the **golden triangle**.
⚠ Gopalan: Art. 21 guards only against the **executive**; Maneka: also against **arbitrary legislation**.

29.s:
Assertion (A): An unguided and uncontrolled discretionary power conferred on an executive authority violates Article 14.
Reason (R): Such discretion subverts the principle of non-arbitrariness and the Rule of Law.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
29.x: Unguided executive discretion violates Article 14 precisely because it is arbitrary and undermines the rule of law, so R explains A.
n: A law conferring unguided discretionary power on an executive authority violates the principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
A law conferring uncontrolled discretionary power on an executive authority violates the principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
A law conferring uncanalized discretionary power on an executive authority violates the principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Unguided executive discretion in applying or enforcing a law directly subverts the Rule of Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Uncontrolled executive discretion in applying or enforcing a law directly subverts the Rule of Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Uncanalized executive discretion in applying or enforcing a law directly subverts the Rule of Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law restrains the government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xa: Discretion without **objective standards** or **judicial safeguards** is **ultra vires** Article 14.
After **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**, procedure must be **"fair, just and reasonable"**.
**A.K. Gopalan (1950)** had accepted any procedure **enacted by the legislature**.

29.s: Which of the following pairs (case – right read into Article 21) is wrongly matched?
o: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) – Privacy
Shafin Jahan (2018) – Marry a person of choice
29.x: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity concerned emergency medical care; privacy was recognised in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).
xa: **Francis Coralie Mullin (1981)** — live with **human dignity**.
**Nilabati Behera (1993)** — **compensation** for violation.
**Chameli Singh (1996)** — **shelter**; **Subhash Kumar (1991)** — **clean environment**.
⚠ **Supriyo Chakraborty (2023):** **no unqualified fundamental right to marry**.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about rights read into Article 21:
1. In Supriyo Chakraborty (2023), the Supreme Court held that there is no fundamental right to marry as such.
2. Compensation for violation of human rights under Article 21 is associated with Nilabati Behera (1993).
3. The right to speedy trial was read into Article 21 in Hussainara Khatoon.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the Court held there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry, while Article 21 protection for dignity, privacy and choice of partner remains.
Statement 2: Correct: Nilabati Behera (1993) is associated with compensation for human rights violations.
Statement 3: Correct: Hussainara Khatoon concerned speedy trial; Maneka Gandhi gave fair procedure and M.H. Hoskot free legal aid.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about the right to die:
1. The Supreme Court decided Common Cause, upholding the living will, in 2018.
2. In Aruna Shanbaug (2011), the Supreme Court held the living will valid.
3. Attempted suicide was decriminalised in effect in 2017, and the BNS has no general offence for it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Common Cause was decided in 2018, after P. Rathinam (1994), Gian Kaur (1996) and Aruna Shanbaug (2011).
Statement 2: Incorrect: Aruna Shanbaug allowed passive euthanasia under High Court supervision; it was Common Cause (2018) that upheld the living will.
Statement 3: Correct: the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised it in effect, and the BNS (in force from 1 July 2024) has no general offence of attempted suicide.

29.s: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from:
29.x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. It does not retain a general offence of attempted suicide corresponding to Section 309 IPC.
29.tq: Date-based recall of the transition from IPC to BNS.
xs: The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** replaced the IPC **from 1 July 2024** — option **(2)**.
After it, **Sec. 309 IPC is history** — there is no general offence of attempted suicide.
xa: **Sec. 226 BNS** punishes only an attempt to **compel or restrain a public servant**.
Double jeopardy: **Sec. 337 BNSS** (earlier **Sec. 300 CrPC**).
Arrest rights: **Secs. 47 and 58 BNSS** (earlier **CrPC 50, 57**).

29.s:
Consider the following statements about the right to education:
1. Article 21A was inserted into the Constitution by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
2. The RTE Act, 2009 reserves 25 per cent of entry-level seats in unaided private schools for children of weaker groups.
3. Section 3 of the Right to Education Act, 2009 gives free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school to every child aged 6 to 16 years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A; the RTE Act, 2009 only gives effect to it.
Statement 2: Correct: the Act provides 25 per cent entry-level seats in unaided private schools for weaker groups, but not in minority schools.
Statement 3: Incorrect: Section 3 covers every child aged 6 to 14 years, not 6 to 16.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about education rights and UAPA bail:
1. The right-to-education case Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka was decided in 1993.
2. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 deleted the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights.
3. With reference to bail in cases under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, the Supreme Court has observed that delay alone is not a trump card for granting bail.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: Mohini Jain was decided in 1992; Unnikrishnan followed in 1993.
Statement 2: Incorrect: the Right to Property was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978; the 86th Amendment changed Articles 21A, 45 and 51A(k).
Statement 3: Correct: the Supreme Court observed on 6 January 2026 that delay alone is not a 'trump card' for bail in UAPA cases.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about arrest and preventive detention:
1. The safeguards in Article 22(1) and 22(2) do not cover a civil arrest or the deportation of an alien.
2. Under Article 22(1), a person arrested and detained in custody has the right to be tried only by a jury.
3. Preventive detention is best described as detention only for non-payment of a civil debt.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Correct: arrest under court orders, civil arrest and deportation of aliens fall outside these safeguards.
Statement 2: Incorrect: Art. 22(1) gives the right to be told the grounds of arrest and to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice; trial by jury is not guaranteed.
Statement 3: Incorrect: preventive detention is detention without trial, on suspicion of future harmful acts.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about preventive detention under Article 22:
1. Under Article 22(7), State Legislatures may prescribe the maximum period of preventive detention.
2. The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 sought to cut the period of preventive detention without an Advisory Board report to two months.
3. Parliament alone can make preventive detention laws on matters connected with defence, foreign affairs and security of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: Article 22(7) permits Parliament, not State Legislatures, to prescribe the maximum period.
Statement 2: Correct: the 44th Amendment cut it from three to two months, but the clause was never notified, so three months still applies under Article 22(4).
Statement 3: Correct: Parliament alone legislates on these matters; Parliament and the States share public order, security of a State and essential supplies.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about preventive detention and arrest:
1. Preventive detention is constitutionally justified under Article 22 in relation to public order, but not merely routine law and order.
2. The National Security Act was enacted in 1980.
3. In Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana (2025), the Supreme Court emphasised that the grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the Supreme Court has distinguished public order from ordinary law and order for preventive detention.
Statement 2: Correct: the National Security Act came in 1980, after the Preventive Detention Act (1950), MISA (1971) and COFEPOSA (1974).
Statement 3: Correct: Vihaan Kumar emphasised that the grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee.

29.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: COFEPOSA, 1974 – Detention up to 12 months without charges
COFEPOSA, 1974 – Detention of suspected smugglers and currency manipulators
29.x: COFEPOSA targets smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators; NSA allows detention up to 12 months without charges and UAPA is the anti-terror law.
xa: **Preventive Detention Act 1950** — first such law; lapsed **1969**.
**MISA 1971** — used in the **Emergency**; repealed **1978**.
SC: delay alone is not a "**trump card**" for bail in **UAPA** cases (**6 Jan 2026**).

29.s: The constitutional status of the Right to Education is best described as follows:
o: It is a Fundamental Duty of parents alone
It is only a Directive Principle of State Policy
It is a statutory right unrelated to Article 21
It is a Fundamental Right and is treated as an extension of the right to life
29.x: The Right to Education is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A and is treated as an extension of the right to life under Article 21.
29.tq: Distinguish the Fundamental Right from the related Directive Principle and parental Fundamental Duty.
xs: Right to education is a **Fundamental Right** (PYQ 2018) and an **extension of the right to life** (**Art. 21**) (PYQ 2019) — option **(4)**.
It sits in **Art. 21A**, inserted by the **86th Amendment, 2002**.
The parents' duty (**51A(k)**) and the DPSP (**Art. 45**) are separate provisions of the same amendment.
xa: **Mohini Jain (1992)** read education into Art. 21 before 21A existed.
**Art. 45** (DPSP): **early childhood care and education** below **6** years.
**51A(k)** is the **11th** Fundamental Duty.

29.s: Compelling to incriminate himself in a case is
29.x: Self incrimination. Compelling a person to become a witness against himself in a criminal case is known as self-incrimination, which is prohibited under Article 20 (3). This protection ensures that no accused person can be forced to confess or provide self-incriminating evidence. It is a key procedural safeguard for individuals facing criminal prosecution.

29.s: According to which Article of the Indian Constitution, 'No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once'?
29.x: Article 20 (2) of the Indian Constitution embodies the principle of protection against double jeopardy, providing that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. Correct Answ (2) (i), (iii) and (iv) Explanation: Article 51A lists the Fundamental Duties of citizens, which explicitly include upholding sovereignty / unity / integrity of India, valuing / preserving the composite culture, and promoting harmony and brotherhood matching (i), (iii) and (iv). ' Protecting the weaker sections from social injustice ' is a State obligation under the Directive Principles, not one of the enumerated fundamental duties of citizens.

29.s: An accused of any offence cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself, which Article of Indian Constitution provides for this ?
29.x: Article 20 has provided a safeguard to the persons accused of crimes. Article 20(3) of the Constitution says that no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to give witness against himself (self-incrimination). This is based on the legal presumption that the accused is innocent till his guilt is proved. It is the duty of the prosecutor to establish his guilt.

29.s: Which Article of the Constitution provides protection to the accused regarding conviction from double-bar and self-incrimination?
29.x: Article 20(2) says that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once, while Article 20(3) describes that no person accused of any offence should be compelled to be a witness against himself.

29.s: “No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.” Under which Article, the above preservation of conviction for crime is given?
29.x: Article 20(2) of the Constitution of India says that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. This is called the ‘Doctrine of Double Jeopardy.’ The objective of this Article is to avoid harassment, which may be caused by successive criminal proceedings where the person has committed one crime. There is a law maxim related to this -Nemo Debet Bis Vexari. This means that no man shall be put twice in peril for the same offence.

29.s: Which one of the following does not fall within the purview of article 21 of the Constitution?
o: Medical aid to injure by a doctor
Sexual Harassment of Women at work place
Pollution of the quality of water
29.x: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution provides that –"No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law." The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has widened the scope and orbit of the right to life and personal liberty on various occasions. According to the question given here, option (d) is correct, as from the decision of Bachan Singh Vs. State of Punjab case, it is now clear that the provision of capital punishment, as given in section 302 of I.P.C., is not violative of Article 21 of the Constitution, because it is given only for serious crimes. So, capital punishment doesn't come under the provision of Article 21 of the Constitution. All the other rights given in the options come under the right to life and personal liberty, as it has been declared by the Supreme Court through following decisions as– (i) Medical aid to the injured by Doctor in Parmananda Katara Vs. Union of India 1989 S.C. (ii) Sexual Harassment of women at workplace in Vishakha Vs. State of Rajasthan 1997 S.C. (iii) Pollution of the quality of Air in Subhash Kumar Vs. State of Bihar 1991 S.C.

29.s: Which Article gives safeguard to the Fundamental Rights of arrested person?
29.x: Article 22 of the Constitution mentions that no arrested person shall be detained in custody without being informed as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest, nor shall he be denied the right to consult and to be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice.

29.s: Which of the following is not a part of the Article 20 of the Constitution of India?
29.x: Prohibition against torture is not part of the Article 20 of the Constitution of India. Protection from torture is a fundamental right enshrined under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution. Article 20 of the Indian Constitution provides protection in respect of conviction for offences : (1) No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of the law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. (2) No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. (3) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.

29.s:
Statement
(A): There is no fundamental right to marry. Statement
(B): Right to travel abroad comes under the purview of Fundamental Rights.
o: Statement (A) is right and Statement (B) is wrong
Statement (A) is wrong and Statement (B) is right
29.x: There is no explicit standalone " fundamental right to marry " in the Constitution (A correct). The Right to Travel Abroad was established under Article 21 through Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India (1978), which expanded " personal liberty " interpretation (B correct).

29.s: Which Article of the Constitution of India safeguards one's right to marry the person of one's choice?
29.x: The Indian Constitution does not explicitly recognize the right to marry as a fundamental or constitutional right. However, through several Supreme Court rulings, the right to marry has been upheld as a fundamental right under Article 21. In Lata Singh v. State of UP (2006), the Supreme Court affirmed that adults have the right to marry anyone they choose, noting that inter-caste marriages are not prohibited by law. Additionally, cases such as Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018) and Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (2018) (Hadiya Marriage Case) reiterated that the choice of a life partner is a key aspect of personal dignity protected under Article 21.

29.s: In essence, what does 'Due Process of Law' mean?
29.x: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, the Supreme Court expanded the meaning of "procedure established by law" to effectively incorporate the concept of due process. It held that any procedure depriving a person of life or personal liberty must be just, fair, and reasonable, and the law itself must also satisfy the requirements of Articles 14, 19, and 21. With this interpretation, both substantive and procedural due process were read into Article 21, thereby embedding the essence of natural justice. Consequently, whenever a person is deprived of life or personal liberty, the guarantees of fairness inherent in natural justice apply. These principles primarily include nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in their own cause, ensuring absence of bias) and audi alteram partem (the right to be heard, meaning no one should be condemned unheard).

29.s: The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
29.x: The 86th CAA, 2002, added the 11th Fundamental Duty requiring parents / guardians to provide educational opportunities to children aged 6- 14, simultaneously introducing Article 21A making free / compulsory education a Fundamental Right for this age group.

29.s: The 93rd Constitution Amendment Bill deals with the:
o: Continuation of reservation for backward classes in
Free and compulsory education for all children
Reservation of 30 percent posts for women in
Allocation of more number of Parliamentary seats for
29.x: The 93rd Constitutional Amendment Bill deals with free and compulsory education for all children between the ages of 6 and 14 years. Through this amendment, a new Article 21-A was added to the Constitution under Fundamental Rights, and Article 45 was amended under the Directive Principles of State Policy; and a new Article 51-A(k) was added to Fundamental Duties. This amendment bill was enacted under the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.

29.s: Right to education to all children between the age group of 6 to 14 years is -
o: Included in the Directive Principles of State Policy
29.x: The Constitution (Eighty-Sixth Amendment) Act, 2002 inserted Article 21-A in the Constitution of India to provide free and compulsory education to all children in the age group of six to fourteen years as a fundamental right in such a manner as the State may, by law, determine. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009, represents the legislation envisaged under Article 21-A. The RTE Act came into effect on 1 April, 2010.

29.s: Which Amendment to the Constitution inserted a new Article 21 A in the Constitution providing Right to Education?
29.x: According to the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 a new Article 21-A was added to the Constitution which made Right to Education a fundamental right for children in the age group of 6-14 years. This Article reads: “The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children between the ages of six and fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.”

29.s: Right to Education has been included into the Fundamental Rights by the

Assertion (A) : The state shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age group of six to fourteen years.
Reason (R) : In a democratic society, right to education is indispensable in the interpretation of the right to development as a human right. In the context of above statements select the correct answer.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct
29.x: According to Article 21A of the Indian Constitution, the state shall provide free and compulsory education to all children between the age of six and fourteen years. Thus, Assertion (A) is true. Education is a fundamental human right and is indispensable in the interpretation of the right to development as a human right, as it promotes individual freedom and empowerment of children. Thus, both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

29.s: ‘Right to Education’ introduced through 86th Amendment came into force:
29.x: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 made education a Fundamental Right through insertion of a new Article 21A. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, enables the implementation of the Fundamental Right, which was passed by the Parliament in

29.s: The scope of the Article 21 of the Constitution was expanded to include Right to Education, because of the decision of Supreme Court in the case
o: Govind v/s State of Madhya Pradesh
Parmanand Katara v/s Union of India
Chameli Singh v/s State of Uttar Pradesh
29.x: The Supreme Court, in the case of 'Unnikrishnan and others versus State of Andhra Pradesh and others', 1993, organised in the form of a right, free education for children upto the age of 14 years. The court held that- The citizens of the country have the fundamental right to education. This right comes out of Article 21. However, the right is not absolute. The content and measures of the right must be determined in light of Articles 41 and 45.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about ‘Right to Education’ and choose the correct answer :
1. It try to achieve the aim of ‘Education for All’.
2. Earlier a provision of free and compulsory education was provided in Part IV of the Constitution.
3. It became Fundamental Right after 91st Constitutional Amendment.
29.x: The ‘Right to Education’ as a Fundamental Right was added through Article 21A by the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002; therefore, linking it to the 91st Amendment is incorrect. In Part IV, the directive provision for free and compulsory education existed in the original Constitution under Article 45; hence, the statement is correct.

29.s: Under Preventive Detention, a person can be detained without trial for –
29.x: According to Article 22(4) of the Indian Constitution, a person can be detained without trial for a maximum period of three months under preventive detention.

1.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Article 28 – Freedom from taxes for promotion of a particular religion
Article 24 – Prohibition of employment of children below 14 in hazardous employment
Article 25 – Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
Article 26 – Right of a religious denomination to manage its religious affairs
1.x: Freedom from taxes for promoting a particular religion is Article 27; Article 28 concerns religious instruction or worship in certain institutions.
xa: **Art. 26** — freedom to **manage religious affairs** (religious denominations).
Right against exploitation = **Arts 23-24**; freedom of religion = **Arts 25-28**.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about Articles 23 to 28:
1. The Right to Freedom of Religion guaranteed under Articles 25 to 28 is classified as a Fundamental Right.
2. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment.
3. Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution together form the Right against Exploitation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Articles 25 to 28 are Fundamental Rights, not merely legal rights or Directive Principles.
Statement 2: Correct: Article 24 bars such employment of children below fourteen; harmless or innocent work is not covered.
Statement 3: Correct: Articles 23–24 form the Right against Exploitation, and Articles 25–28 the Right to Freedom of Religion.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about exploitation and religious freedom:
1. The protection against trafficking and forced labour under Article 23 is available only when the exploitation is committed by a public authority.
2. Under the Child Labour Amendment Act, 2016, adolescents aged 14–18 years are barred from hazardous work.
3. The text 'All persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion' is found in Article 25(1).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: Article 23 protects citizens and non-citizens and operates against the State as well as private persons.
Statement 2: Correct: the 2016 amendment bars adolescents aged 14–18 from hazardous work.
Statement 3: Correct: these words are Article 25(1), subject to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about Articles 26 to 28:
1. The right under Article 27 is available to all persons, citizens and foreigners.
2. Under Article 28(3), attendance at religious instruction can be made compulsory in State-aided institutions.
3. The Supreme Court has left it to the Ministry of Education to decide whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under Article 26(a).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Article 27, like Articles 25 and 28, is available to all persons; Article 26 is available to religious denominations.
Statement 2: Incorrect: Article 28(3) protects freedom from compulsory attendance; no person can be compelled to attend religious instruction without consent.
Statement 3: Correct: the question left to the Ministry is whether such schools fall under Article 26(a), rather than Articles 19(1)(g) or 30(1).

1.s:
Consider the following statements about secularism and religion:
1. In a theocratic state, an official religion guides law and State policy.
2. Non-applicability of secular principles to irreligious persons is not a component of Indian secularism.
3. Emile Durkheim regarded religion as a form of collective worship of society and examined the distinction between the sacred and the profane.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Correct: a theocratic state has an official religion that guides its law and policy; this is not a feature of the Indian Constitution.
Statement 2: Correct: secularism includes freedom of conscience, which protects believers as well as non-believers.
Statement 3: Correct: Durkheim associated religion with collective worship of society and distinguished the sacred from the profane.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about religion in Indian society:
1. In July 2026, the Ravidassias renewed their demand for a separate religion code in the Census.
2. Max Weber linked karma, dharma and caste with the shaping of economic life in The Religion of India.
3. In Hinduism, Karma refers to duty or righteous conduct.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the Ravidassias renewed their demand for a separate religion code in the Census in July 2026.
Statement 2: Correct: Max Weber examined the relationship of karma, dharma and caste to economic life in The Religion of India.
Statement 3: Incorrect: Karma is the law of action and consequence; duty is Dharma.

1.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 21A provides the Right to Education.
2. Article 24 prohibits employment of children in factories and similar establishments.
3. Article 27 provides freedom to manage religious affairs.
Which of the above statements are correct?
1.x: Article 21A gives the Right to Education and Article 24 bars child labour; freedom to manage religious affairs is Article 26, while Article 27 concerns taxes for promoting religion.
n: Article 21-A provides the Right to Education. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Article 24 prohibits the employment of children in factories and similar establishments. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Article 26 provides freedom to manage religious affairs. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Article 27 provides freedom from payment of taxes for the promotion of any religion. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Child labour is prohibited below the age of 14 years under Article 24. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
xa: **Article 25** = freedom of **conscience** and to **profess, practise and propagate** religion.
**Article 28** = freedom from attending **religious instruction** in certain institutions.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 23:

2. 'Begar', as used in the context of Article 23, means unpaid forced labour exacted by officials or zamindars.
3. Article 23(2) does not require the State to pay remuneration in every case of compulsory service.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour; Article 23(2) is the exception for compulsory public service.
Statement 2: Correct: begar refers to unpaid forced labour traditionally exacted by officials or zamindars.
Statement 3: Correct: Article 23(2) does not require payment in every case of compulsory public service.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about child protection and Bhakti:
1. Articles 21A and 24 together most directly strengthen the constitutional protection of children against exploitation by combining education and child-labour safeguards.
2. Articles 39(e) and 39(f) are the Directive Principles that direct the State to ensure that the tender age of children is not abused and that children are protected against exploitation.
3. The Bhakti movement, which rejected ritualism and caste, spans roughly the 3rd to 8th century.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Article 21A provides free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14, while Article 24 bars their employment in factories, mines and hazardous work.
Statement 2: Correct: Articles 39(e) and 39(f) protect children's tender age from abuse and ensure healthy development free from exploitation.
Statement 3: Incorrect: Bhakti spans the 6th to the 18th century.

1.s:

2. Trafficking is dealt with under Section 143 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
3. The NCPCR and the SCPCRs are constituted under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act is of 1976; ITPA is of 1956 and the Child Labour Act of 1986.
Statement 2: Correct: Section 143 of the BNS, in force from 1 July 2024, deals with trafficking; victim consent is immaterial.
Statement 3: Correct: NCPCR and SCPCRs are set up under the 2005 Act; POCSO 2012 and ITPA 1956 do not create the commissions.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 25:
1. In Article 25(1), 'propagate' means spreading one's beliefs to others, while the inner freedom to mould one's relation with God is conscience.
2. The freedoms in Article 25(1) are subject to public order, morality, health and security of the State.
3. Article 25(2)(a) lets the State regulate secular activity associated with religion, not spiritual belief.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Correct: propagate means spreading one's beliefs to others; the inner freedom to mould one's relation with God is conscience.
Statement 2: Incorrect: Article 25(1) subjects these freedoms to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III.
Statement 3: Correct: Article 25(2)(a) reaches secular activity associated with religion, not spiritual belief.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about Articles 25 and 26:
1. For Article 25(2)(b), the expression 'Hindus' includes Sikhs and Jains only.
2. Where a religious practice involves a social evil, the State must leave reform entirely to the religious denomination.
3. The rights of religious denominations under Article 26 are subject to public order, morality and health.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: the explanation to Article 25 includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists within 'Hindus'.
Statement 2: Incorrect: freedom of religion is not absolute; the State may intervene to root out social evils, subject to constitutional limits.
Statement 3: Correct: Article 26 rights to set up institutions and own and administer property are expressly subject to public order, morality and health.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about religious pluralism and faiths:

2. In Buddhism, the Tripitaka refers to the sacred texts.
3. In Jainism, Sallekhana refers to a ritual fast unto death.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

Statement 1: Incorrect: freedom to practise any religion or none is what religious pluralism rests on; exclusivism hinders it.
Statement 2: Correct: the Tripitaka is the Buddhist sacred texts; the Sangha is the monastic order.
Statement 3: Correct: Sallekhana is the Jain ritual fast unto death; Kaivalya is liberation.

1.s:
Consider the following statements about Indian secularism:
1. The constitutional meaning of secularism in India is best described as the establishment of one official religion by the State.
2. Indian secularism is best described as a state religion with tolerance of other faiths.
3. Unlike the Western model of strict separation, Indian secularism is based on principled distance and equal respect.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: Indian secularism means equal respect for all religions and no discrimination on religious grounds; it does not establish a state religion.
Statement 2: Incorrect: India has no state religion and allows positive state intervention for social and religious reform.
Statement 3: Correct: the Western model rests on strict separation and mutual exclusion, while the Indian model adopts principled distance, equal respect and scope for reform.

1.s:

1.x:

Statement 2: Correct: the Constituent Assembly rejected the proposal to add the word "God" to the Preamble in 1949.
Statement 3: Correct: Ashoka's Dhamma, the Nehru Report (1928) and the Karachi Resolution (1931) are all identified as roots of Indian secular thought.

1.s:

2. The S.R. Bommai case (1994) held secularism to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

Statement 3: Incorrect: communalism, separatism and fanaticism are all identified as forms of religious fundamentalism in India, not only communalism and fanaticism.

30.s: Which of the following Article is called the "Heart and Soul" of the Indian Constitution?
30.x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described Article 32 of the Indian Constitution as its “heart and soul” because it safeguards fundamental rights and ensures justice for all citizens. This article empowers individuals to directly approach the Supreme Court if their fundamental rights are violated, ensures that the government respects individual freedoms and establishes the protection of fundamental rights as a fundamental right itself.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 32:
1. Under clause (4) of Article 32, the right cannot be suspended by an ordinary law of Parliament.
2. Article 226 lets Parliament empower any other court to exercise the Supreme Court's powers under Article 32.
3. Article 32 is a statutory remedy that Parliament may withdraw.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Article 32(4) says the right cannot be suspended except as the Constitution provides, not by an ordinary law.
Statement 2: Incorrect: it is Article 32(3), not Article 226, that permits Parliament to empower other courts; High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
Statement 3: Incorrect: Article 32 is part of the basic structure and cannot be abridged even by a constitutional amendment.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 32 and the writs:
1. The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 is appellate and exclusive.
2. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described Article 19 as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
3. The writ of Habeas Corpus may be directed against both public authorities and private individuals.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: the jurisdiction is original but not exclusive, because High Courts also exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
Statement 2: Incorrect: Dr. Ambedkar described Article 32, not Article 19, as the heart and soul of the Constitution.
Statement 3: Correct: Habeas Corpus lies against public authorities and private individuals for unlawful detention.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about writs and writ jurisdiction:
1. The writ of Quo Warranto lies against the holder of a substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution.
2. Before 1950, writ jurisdiction was exercised by the High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.
3. Article 32(2) specifically recognises three writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Quo Warranto tests a claim to a substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution.
Statement 2: Correct: before 1950 only the Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts had writ jurisdiction; Article 226 now empowers all High Courts.
Statement 3: Incorrect: Article 32(2) refers to five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the scope of writs:
1. As a general rule, the writ of mandamus is not issued against a private individual or body.
2. Certiorari can be used in relation to a pending proceeding, to transfer a pending case.
3. A High Court may issue a writ beyond its territorial limits under Article 226 when the Supreme Court authorises it in every individual case.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x:
Statement 1: Correct: mandamus is not ordinarily issued against private bodies, nor for discretionary or legislative functions.
Statement 2: Correct: certiorari is generally post-decision, but it may also be used to transfer a pending case.
Statement 3: Incorrect: a High Court may do so where the cause of action wholly or partly arises within its territory, a position that followed the Fifteenth Amendment of 1963.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about writs and Public Interest Litigation:
1. Both the Supreme Court and the High Courts can issue all five writs, not five and three respectively.
2. Public Interest Litigation primarily relaxes the rule that judicial review is unavailable against administrative action.
3. The 1981 case associated with the development of Public Interest Litigation is Maneka Gandhi.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x:
Statement 1: Correct: both the Supreme Court and the High Courts can issue all five writs.
Statement 2: Incorrect: PIL relaxes the rule of locus standi, that only the directly aggrieved person may approach the court.
Statement 3: Incorrect: the 1981 PIL case is S.P. Gupta, not Maneka Gandhi.

30.s: A Writ of Prohibition is an order issued by the Supreme Court or High Courts to :
o: a government officer prohibiting him from taking a

30.x: The Writ of Prohibition is a legal term that implies "to prohibit, prevent, forbid, or restrain". It is a legal remedy that can be sought from a higher court to prevent a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction or acting unlawfully. It is a command issued by a superior court to a lower court, directing it to cease proceedings that are beyond its legal authority or contrary to the principles of natural justice. In essence, the writ of prohibition serves as a check on the power of lower courts or tribunals, ensuring that they operate within the boundaries of their jurisdiction and adhere to the principles of justice. It acts as a mechanism to correct errors and prevent potential harm that may arise from biased or unfair proceedings. It cannot be enforced against administrative agencies, statutory authorities, or private persons or enterprises. It is exclusively applicable to judicial and quasi-judicial bodies. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

31.s:
Assertion (A): The Directive Principles cannot be enforced by any court.

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
31.x: Both are true and R explains A: courts cannot enforce the Directive Principles because Article 37 declares them non-justiciable, though fundamental in governance.

n: The Directive Principles of State Policy are non-justiciable. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]

xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Article 37**: Part IV "**shall not be enforceable by any court**" — this is why DPSPs are **non-justiciable**.
Yet they are "**fundamental in the governance of the country**" and the State must apply them in making laws.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G2 **2025** A-R: DPSPs as a **guidepost for legislation** does **not** explain non-enforceability — that flows from **Art. 37**.
FRs carry a **legal** sanction; DPSPs a **moral and political** sanction.

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
31.x: All are correct: Directive Principles of State Policy: Article 45 directs the state to provide for early childhood care and education for children below the age of six. • Rural and Urban Local Bodies: The Eleventh Schedule includes education, including primary and secondary schools, among the responsibilities entrusted to Panchayats. • Fifth Schedule: The provisions of the Fifth Schedule shall apply to the administration and control of the Scheduled Areas and Tribes in any State other than the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. PESA,1996 was enacted for tribal self-rule in India's scheduled areas. The Act has contributed to the improvement of access to basic services, such as education, healthcare, and drinking water, in the Scheduled Areas. • Sixth Schedule: It contains special provisions for the tribal areas in the four north-eastern states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. There are 10 such 'tribal areas' at present in these four States.  Under this, the district council can establish, construct or manage primary schools, dispensaries, markets, ferries, fisheries, roads and so on in the district. It can also make regulations to control moneylending and trading by non-tribals. But such regulations require the governor's assent. • Seventh Schedule: Initially, education was under the State List, but the 42 ND Amendment Act of 1976 moved it to the Concurrent List, shared between the Centre and states.

o: the Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy

The DPSPs (Part IV of the Constitution) contain provisions aimed at achieving economic justice, such as: • Article 38: Direct the state to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order permeated by justice– social, economic and political–and to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities • Article 39: The State shall ensure that the ownership and control of resources are distributed to serve the common good and that citizens have an adequate means of livelihood. • Articles 41, 42, 43, etc., promote workers' rights, equal pay, and equitable distribution of resources.

31.s: According to the Constitution of India, which of the following are fundamental for the governance of the country?
31.x: Indian Polity: Constitutional Framework PMF IAS IP – 25 The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), as outlined in Part IV of the Constitution of India, are fundamental in the governance of the country. While they are not justiciable (i.e., they cannot be enforced by the courts), they serve as guidelines to the government in formulating policies and laws aimed at promoting social justice and welfare.

31.s: The ideal of 'Welfare State' in the Indian Constitution is enshrined in its

32.s:
Consider the following statements about Fundamental Rights versus DPSP:
1. Fundamental Rights are mostly negative, restraining the State, while Directive Principles are positive directions to the State.
2. A law violating a Fundamental Right cannot be examined by courts, while a law violating a Directive Principle is void under Article 37.
3. The first case of conflict between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles was Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x:
Statement 1: Correct: FRs are mostly negative and aim at political democracy; DPSPs are positive and aim at social and economic democracy.
Statement 2: Incorrect: a law violating a Fundamental Right may be void under Article 13, while a law cannot be struck down merely for violating a Directive Principle.
Statement 3: Incorrect: the first conflict case was Champakam Dorairajan (1951), not Kesavananda Bharati.

32.s:
Assertion (A): Article 48A read with Article 21 has been used to support the right to a healthy environment.
Reason (R): Directive Principles are entirely excluded from constitutional interpretation because they are non-justiciable.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
32.x: Courts use Directive Principles to enrich Fundamental Rights (e.g. Article 48A with 21, Article 45 with 21); non-justiciability does not exclude them from interpretation.
xa: Validity test for a DPSP law abridging FRs: the **basic structure** + **golden triangle** (Arts **14, 19, 21**).
FRs and DPSPs: **FRs are means, DPSPs are the ends**.
**Justice Chandrachud**: together they are the **conscience of the Constitution**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about FR-DPSP landmark cases:
1. State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) did not adopt harmonious construction under which DPSPs prevail over Fundamental Rights.
2. In re Kerala Education Bill, 1958 is associated with Parliament's inability to amend any Fundamental Right.
3. Golaknath (1967) denied Parliament the power to amend Fundamental Rights and applied the doctrine of prospective overruling.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x:
Statement 1: Correct: harmonious construction came in In re Kerala Education Bill (1958), and even there Fundamental Rights still prevail.
Statement 2: Incorrect: In re Kerala Education Bill adopted harmonious construction, giving effect to both Parts III and IV as far as possible.
Statement 3: Correct: Golaknath (1967) gave FRs a 'transcendental' position and applied prospective overruling.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about landmark constitutional cases:
1. Minerva Mills was decided in 1980.
2. A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) gave a narrow interpretation of Article 21.
3. The Minerva Mills case expanded the scope of Article 21 through due process.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Minerva Mills (1980) came after Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and before Sanjeev Coke (1983).
Statement 2: Correct: A.K. Gopalan (1950) read Article 21 narrowly.
Statement 3: Incorrect: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21 through due process; Minerva Mills dealt with amending power.

32.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Minerva Mills (1980) – Fundamental Rights are superior to DPSP
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) – Balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP
Golaknath (1967) – Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights
32.x: Golaknath held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. Champakam: FRs above DPSP; Kesavananda: Basic Structure; Minerva Mills: balance between FRs and DPSP.
n: The Champakam Dorairajan case held that Fundamental Rights are superior to Directive Principles. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
The Golaknath case held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
The Kesavananda Bharati case established the Basic Structure principle. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]

Directive Principles are subordinate to Fundamental Rights, with exceptions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
The Minerva Mills case held that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are equally important. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xa: **Kerala Education Bill (1958)** = **harmonious construction**.
**Sanjeev Coke (1983)** read "material resources" to include **privately owned** resources.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about amendments answering court rulings:
1. Article 15(4), inserted by the First Amendment Act, 1951, was a response to the Champakam Dorairajan judgment.
2. Article 31C was inserted into the Constitution by the Seventeenth Amendment.
3. The Twenty-fourth Amendment Act, 1971, enacted in response to Golaknath, provided that Parliament could amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x:
Statement 1: Correct: Article 15(4) answered Champakam Dorairajan.
Statement 2: Incorrect: Article 31C came with the Twenty-fifth Amendment; the Seventeenth widened 'estate' in Article 31A.
Statement 3: Correct: the Twenty-fourth Amendment affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, adding Articles 13(4) and 368(3).

32.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Twenty-fifth Amendment — inserted Article 31C and replaced ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’
Twenty-sixth Amendment — extended Article 31C to all DPSPs
32.x: The Twenty-fifth Amendment replaced ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’ and inserted Article 31C. The Twenty-fourth Amendment dealt with Parliament's amending power, the Twenty-sixth abolished privy purses, and the Forty-second extended Article 31C to all DPSPs.
32.tq: Start from the sure amendment-provision pair and reject swapped amendment responses.
xs: The **25th Amendment** inserted **Art. 31C** and replaced **compensation** by **amount** — option **(1)**.
The **24th** dealt with Parliament's power to amend FRs; the **26th** abolished **privy purses**.
The **42nd** extended 31C to all DPSPs; **Art. 15(4)** came by the **1st Amendment (1951)**.
xa: The 25th responded to the **Bank Nationalisation** case (**R.C. Cooper, 1970**).
Original 31C protected **39(b) and (c)** laws from **Arts 14, 19** (and 31).
**Kesavananda (1973)** struck down the **second provision** of 31C (bar on judicial review).

32.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 31C and related cases:
1. The 42nd Amendment attempted to extend Article 31C protection to laws implementing all the Directive Principles.
2. It is not correct that Article 31C was introduced by the 25th Amendment in 1971.
3. I.R. Coelho, the last word on the Ninth Schedule, was decided in 2007.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the 42nd Amendment, not the 44th, attempted the extension, and it was struck down by the Supreme Court.
Statement 2: Incorrect: the claim that is not correct about Article 31C is that Minerva Mills upheld the 42nd Amendment's extension; Minerva Mills struck it down.
Statement 3: Correct: I.R. Coelho came in 2007.

32.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule is NOT correct?
o: Article 31B was inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951
The Ninth Schedule has remained confined to land reform laws and never expanded beyond them
The number of entries in it grew to more than 280
The Ninth Schedule was initially associated with protection for land reform laws from Fundamental Rights challenges
32.x: Option B is the incorrect statement: the Ninth Schedule, though created by the 1st Amendment, 1951 (Art. 31B) to shield land-reform laws, later grew to over 280 entries and did not stay confined to land reforms. Options A, C and D are correct statements.
32.tq: Reject the absolute claim that an initially limited constitutional device never expanded.
xs: The incorrect statement is that the Ninth Schedule **stayed confined to land reform** — option **(2)**.
It was meant for **land reforms**, but grew to **over 280 entries**.
**Art. 31B** and the Ninth Schedule came with the **1st Amendment, 1951** — (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: **Waman Rao (1981)**: entries after **24 April 1973** open to challenge.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: **no blanket immunity**; the **last word** on the Ninth Schedule.
**Reservation acts** placed in the Ninth Schedule are open to **judicial review**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 31C and early amendments:
1. The First Constitutional Amendment Act, which added Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule, was enacted in 1950.
2. The original Article 31C protected laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31.
3. In Kesavananda Bharati, the first provision of Article 31C was upheld and the second provision was struck down.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x:
Statement 1: Incorrect: the 1st Amendment was enacted in 1951, not 1950.
Statement 2: Correct: the original Article 31C shielded such laws from Articles 14, 19 and 31.
Statement 3: Correct: Kesavananda Bharati upheld the first part of Article 31C but struck down the second, which excluded judicial review.

32.s: In Waman Rao (1981), laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after which date were held open to challenge?
32.x: Waman Rao used 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda judgment, as the cut-off; I.R. Coelho (2007) rejected blanket immunity.
xa: Arts 14, 19, 21 are the **golden triangle**.
**Art. 31B** (**1st Amendment, 1951**) shields Ninth Schedule laws; entries grew to **over 280**.
I.R. Coelho is the **last word** on the Ninth Schedule.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about Article 39(b) and material resources:
1. The continued operation of the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, was reaffirmed in 2024 in the Property Owners Association decision.
2. According to the latest Supreme Court position, whether a privately owned resource is a "material resource of the community" under Article 39(b) depends on factors such as its nature, scarcity, effect on community well-being and the consequences of concentration in private hands.
3. The 7:2 majority opinion in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024) was written by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x:
Statement 1: Correct: the Property Owners Association decision of 2024 affirmed that the original Article 31C continues in force.
Statement 2: Correct: the Court held that private ownership alone does not automatically bring a resource within Article 39(b); it depends on the resource and its effects.
Statement 3: Correct: CJI D.Y. Chandrachud wrote the nine-judge Bench's majority, rejecting Justice Krishna Iyer's 1977 Ranganatha Reddy minority view.

32.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the judicial history of Article 39(b)?
o: Property Owners Association held that every privately owned resource automatically falls within Article 39(b)
In Ranganatha Reddy (1977), Justice Krishna Iyer's minority view included privately owned resources in 'material resources of the community'
The broad view was followed in Sanjeev Coke (1983)
Property Owners Association was decided in 2024
32.x: The 2024 Property Owners Association decision rejected the proposition that every privately owned resource automatically falls within Article 39(b).
xa: The 2024 test: the resource's **nature, scarcity**, effect on community well-being, consequences of **concentration**.
It was a **9-judge** Bench, **7:2**, majority by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**.
Sanjeev Coke upheld **coking coal nationalisation** under 39(b) / 31C.

32.s: With reference to the constitutional status of Directive Principles, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: They are legally superior to all Fundamental Rights in every circumstance
They are enforceable only during a national emergency
They have no constitutional significance because Article 37 excludes them from governance
They are not enforceable in courts but are fundamental in the governance of the country
32.x: Directive Principles are non-justiciable, but Article 37 declares them fundamental in the governance of the country and makes it the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.
32.tq: Avoid the trap of equating non-enforceability with lack of constitutional importance.
xs: DPSPs are **not enforceable in courts** but are **fundamental in the governance** of the country — option **(4)**.
**Art. 37** bars court enforcement, yet declares them fundamental in governance, so (3) is wrong.
(1) is wrong: FRs are legally **superior**; DPSPs are **non-justiciable**.
xa: Main difference (**UPSC 2009**): DPSPs are **not enforceable** in courts, FRs are.
Relationship: **complementary, not competing** — an **integrated scheme**.
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: **balance** between Parts III and IV is part of the **Basic Structure**.

32.s: The Ninth Schedule was introduced in the Constitution of India during the prime ministership of Indian Polity: Constitutional Framework PMF IAS IP – 36
32.x: The Ninth Schedule of the Constitution of India was introduced during the prime ministership of Jawaharlal Nehru through the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951. It was added by inserting Article 31B, which, along with Article 31A, aimed to protect laws related to agrarian reforms from judicial review and facilitate the abolition of the Zamindari system.

32.s: The statement “Fundamental Rights are the means and Directive Principles are the ends” signifies that
o: Fundamental Rights provide the framework through which the social and economic objectives of Directive Principles may be pursued
Directive Principles have no relationship with Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights may be suspended whenever a Directive Principle is invoked
Directive Principles are enforceable through the same remedies as Fundamental Rights
32.x: Fundamental Rights provide rights-based means, while Directive Principles express broader social and economic goals. The two are therefore to be understood together, not as competing constitutional compartments.
32.tq: Translate a constitutional maxim into its practical relationship between rights and goals.
xs: FRs provide the **framework (means)** through which the social and economic **objectives (ends)** of DPSPs are pursued — option **(1)**.
The notes describe FRs and DPSPs as **complementary, not competing** — an **integrated scheme** — so (2) is wrong.
DPSPs are **non-justiciable** (**Art. 37**), so they are not enforced through FR remedies — (4) is wrong.
xa: **Justice Chandrachud**: FRs and DPSPs together = the **conscience of the Constitution**.
**Harmonious construction**: give effect to both as far as possible (**Kerala Education Bill, 1958**).
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: absolute primacy to either Part destroys the **balance**, which is part of the **Basic Structure**.

32.s: In which of the following cases did the Supreme Court of India declare the prevalence of Fundamental rights over Directive Principles of the State Policy in case of conflict between the two?
o: The State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
Kesavananda Bharati v. the State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. the Union of India (1980)
32.x: In the State of Madras Vs Champakam Dorairajan (1951) case, the Supreme Court of India held that, in the case of conflict between these two, the fundamental right shall prevail over the Directive Principles of State policy. It is notable that the state of Madras issued orders for community-based reservation for Medical College seats, in the furtherance of Article 46 of the Directive Principles of State Policy. The said order was challenged on the grounds of violation of fundamental rights under Article 15(1) and Article 29(2). The Supreme Court in its decision, hailed the superiority of the fundamental rights over the directive principles and cancelled the Madras government’s order of community based reservation. To remove the effect of this decision the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 added clause (4) to the Article 15 under fundamental rights. This clause (4) of Article 15 established that, nothing in Article 15 or clause (2) of Article 29 shall prevent the state from making any provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

o: Protection of agrarian reforms in certain States
